Direct answer: a maximum notice period of two months, a transitional period of up to 30 calendar days (extendable once, or up to seven months if 30 days is technically unfeasible), and yes — in March 2026 the provider may still impose reduced switching charges.

- Article 25(2)(d): the contract may set a maximum notice period for initiating the switching process, which shall not exceed two months.
- Article 25(2)(a): the switching must occur within the mandatory maximum transitional period of 30 calendar days, initiated after the maximum notice period, during which the contract remains applicable and the provider must assist the customer and maintain business continuity.
- Article 25(4): if the 30-day period is technically unfeasible, the provider must notify the customer within 14 working days, justify this, and indicate an alternative transitional period not exceeding seven months, with service continuity ensured.
- Article 25(5): the customer has the right to extend the transitional period once for a period it considers more appropriate for its own purposes.
- Article 29(2)–(3): from 11 January 2024 to 12 January 2027, providers may impose reduced switching charges, which shall not exceed the costs directly linked to the switching process concerned — so charges are still permissible in March 2026 (they are banned only from 12 January 2027, Article 29(1)).

No, it cannot be registered. Under Article 18(c), an entity must operate on a not-for-profit basis and be legally independent from any entity that operates on a for-profit basis; a foundation legally controlled by a for-profit pharmaceutical group fails this requirement.

For a qualifying entity: under Article 19(5), once it has submitted all necessary information under Article 19(4) and the competent authority has evaluated the application and found it complies with Article 18, the authority must register it in the public national register within 12 weeks after receipt of the application. That registration is valid in all Member States, and the competent authority must notify the Commission, which includes the registration in the public Union register (Article 19(5)).

Data Governance Act - definition of 'data holder': a legal person, including public sector bodies and international organisations, or a natural person who is not a data subject with respect to the specific data in question, which, in accordance with applicable Union or national law, has the right to grant access to or to share certain personal data or non-personal data.
Data Act - definition of 'data holder': a natural or legal person that has the right or obligation, in accordance with this Regulation, applicable Union law or national legislation adopted in accordance with Union law, to use and make available data, including, where contractually agreed, product data or related service data which it has retrieved or generated during the provision of a related service.

Both definitions allow a natural person to be a data holder, but the DGA restricts this to a natural person who is not a data subject with respect to the specific data, whereas the Data Act allows any natural or legal person without that restriction. As to the basis of the status, the DGA requires only a right to grant access to or share data under applicable Union or national law, while the Data Act requires a right or obligation to use and make available data under the Data Act itself, applicable Union law or national legislation adopted in accordance with Union law.
